result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.neighbors()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get neighbors of a node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9834-L9973){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.neighbors( node, mode="out", ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Neighbors](/assets/graphs/neighbors.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node directed graph with the query node C outlined. With mode all, every node joined to C by an edge in either direction is returned, so B, D, A, and E and their edges to C are in the accent color. The card lists B, D, A, E: successors first, then predecessors." width="100%"} Returns the IDs of the nodes directly connected to a given node, with control over edge direction in directed graphs. This is the basic building block for exploring a graph locally, for example to: - list someone's contacts, followers, or followees in a social network - walk outward from a node in a custom traversal or random walk - compare the neighborhoods of two nodes (e.g. to find common neighbors) How the three modes behave: - `"out"` (default): nodes reached by edges leaving the node (successors), read from the adjacency list in edge insertion order. For undirected graphs this already gives every neighbor, whichever way round each edge was added. - `"in"`: nodes with an edge pointing into the node (predecessors), found by scanning the edge list. Each predecessor is listed once. - `"all"`: the `"out"` result followed by any predecessors not already in it. The `"out"` list has one entry per edge, so a node joined by parallel edges appears more than once, and a self-loop lists the node itself (twice in an undirected graph). Wrap the result in `set()` if you need distinct neighbors. In undirected graphs, use the default `mode="out"` (or `"all"`): `mode="in"` only matches edges that were added with the node as `target=`, so it can miss neighbors. Because `"in"` and `"all"` scan every edge, they are slower than `"out"` on large graphs; `get_predecessors()` and `get_successors()` are dedicated alternatives for directed graphs. The current selection is ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node whose neighbors to find, as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). [mode]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["out"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which edges to follow: `"out"` (default) for outgoing edges (successors), `"in"` for incoming edges (predecessors), or `"all"` for both. In undirected graphs, `"out"` and `"all"` return the same neighbors. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of neighbor node IDs, in edge insertion order (for `mode="all"`, successors first, then predecessors). Use `get_label_from_id()` to convert them to labels. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `mode=` is not one of `"out"`, `"in"`, or `"all"`, or if `node=` is a label that doesn't belong to any node. [KeyError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is an integer ID that doesn't exist and `mode=` is `"out"` or `"all"`. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is neither an `int` nor a `str`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} By default, `mode="out"` returns only outgoing neighbors -- here node "A"'s only outgoing edge points to "B": ::: {#61e7060e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "A")]) ) out_neighbors = graph.neighbors("A", mode="out") out_neighbors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [2] ``` ::: ::: `mode="in"` instead follows incoming edges -- "C" points to "A", so it's the only predecessor: ::: {#ba2b5530 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.neighbors("A", mode="in") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [3] ``` ::: ::: `mode="all"` combines both directions, listing the successor "B" before the predecessor "C": ::: {#54cb3bbc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.neighbors("A", mode="all") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [2, 3] ``` ::: ::: Since results are node IDs rather than labels, map them back with `get_label_from_id()` when a human-readable answer is needed: ::: {#b55f1adc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.neighbors("A", mode="all")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['B', 'C'] ``` ::: ::: In an undirected graph, the default mode returns every neighbor regardless of how the edges were added. A parallel edge makes "B" appear twice; `set()` removes the repeat: ::: {#b9f6e885 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["Ann", "Bob", "Cat"]) .add_edges( [ ("Ann", "Bob"), ("Cat", "Ann"), ("Ann", "Bob"), # parallel edge ] ) ) nbrs = friends.neighbors("Ann") [friends.get_label_from_id(n) for n in nbrs], len(set(nbrs)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (['Bob', 'Cat', 'Bob'], 2) ``` ::: :::
